analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Dodd-Frank law that reined in Wall Street after the 2008 financial crisis.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 22 Republican senators, never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the Dodd-Frank Act, the 2010 law passed after the 2008 financial crisis that tightened rules on banks, created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, restricted risky trading by federally insured banks, and created a process for winding down failing big financial firms without taxpayer bailouts. Repealing it would return banking to the looser rules that were in place before the crisis. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Large banks and other financial firms would gain the most: they would be freed from the capital, trading, derivatives, and consumer-protection rules imposed by Dodd-Frank, reducing their compliance costs and reopening profitable but riskier lines of business. Riskier consumer lenders, who would no longer face the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, would also benefit. Some community banks would gain relief from compliance paperwork, though they would also lose the exemptions and stability rules the law gave them.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Dodd-Frank Act in its entirety and restores the prior law as if it had never been enacted [S2] [S3].
Repeal would remove the law's rules on bank capital, trading, derivatives markets, securities, consumer credit, and foreign banking, since all of those were subjects the law amended [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers and taxpayers would bear the cost if it passed: they would lose the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and other consumer protections, and the financial system would return to the pre-crisis rules associated with the 2008 meltdown, whose costs when banks fail fall on depositors, borrowers, and ultimately taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would eliminate the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and other consumer protections covering mortgages, credit cards, and other consumer credit, returning borrowers to the pre-2010 rules [S2] [S3].

Repeal would strip away the law's rules on the largest banks, derivatives markets, and the wind-down process for failing financial firms, restoring the legal framework in place before the 2008 crisis [S2] [S3].

The strongest good-faith case for repeal was that Dodd-Frank's compliance burden weighs heavily on smaller banks and that the law did not end federal backing for the largest firms; a full repeal, however, would have removed the consumer protections and wind-down tools along with the paperwork.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is compliance relief, which matters most to smaller lenders. The cost is removing the entire post-crisis regulatory framework at once, including consumer protections and the process for resolving failing big firms. Most observers across the debate favored targeted changes rather than a full repeal, which is one reason this bill drew no Democratic support and never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in February 2013, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator David Vitter introduced the bill with 19 original Republican cosponsors on February 27, 2013 [S3] [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No further action was ever recorded; the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers and taxpayers came out ahead in the narrow sense that the post-crisis rules on banks, and the consumer protections created by Dodd-Frank, remained on the books. The bill's backers, who wanted the whole law repealed, gained nothing; the financial industry's preferred outcome of full repeal did not happen.

for.name: Sen. David Vitter
for.role: U.S. Senator from Louisiana; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal Dodd-Frank in its entirety

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Max Baucus (D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or a vote on the bill during the two-year Congress

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill.

industries.note: Full repeal would have freed them from Dodd-Frank's capital, trading, derivatives, and resolution rules, cutting compliance costs and reopening riskier business lines. The downside of those risks, when banks fail, falls on depositors, borrowers, and taxpayers.
Repeal would abolish the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, ending the main federal watchdog over mortgages, credit cards, and collection practices.

Repeal would lift compliance paperwork that falls heavily on small lenders, but it would also remove the stability rules and crisis-era framework those banks operate under, and would reopen the risky environment that damaged the sector in 2008.
